preamble: One historic figure and 10 possible compatriots are clued without further definition

clue.text: A long time undercover

indicators.note: read as two words, under cover: something beneath a covering sits inside it, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: the cover part of the word: a lid covers a pot or box
an eon is an immeasurably long period

explanation.surface: An agent who has spent years working undercover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undercover' reads as one word for a spy, but split it: the long time goes under, inside, the cover.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Leonid, as in Brezhnev, is a Russian first name, so a possible compatriot of Lenin.

clue.text: Language completely covered by networks

indicators.note: something covered by another thing is wrapped up inside it

parts.note: LANs are local area networks
all = completely, wholly

explanation.surface: A language that is entirely carried over computer networks.
explanation.walkthrough: LAN is the standard abbreviation for a local area network, a small computer network.
explanation.definitionFit: Lallans is the Lowland Scots tongue, a literary name for the Scots dialect spoken south of the Highlands.

clue.text: Hence, perhaps, Japanese sailor: his other name is?

definitions.note: a place from which someone might come, so 'hence' (from here) points to a city

parts.note: OS is an ordinary seaman
aka, 'also known as', introduces another name

explanation.surface: Puzzling over the alias of a Japanese seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Japanese sailor' looks like one unit, but 'Japanese' belongs with 'Hence, perhaps': hence means from here, and a person from this place would perhaps be Japanese.
explanation.definitionFit: Osaka is a major port city in Japan, so being from there would make you Japanese.

clue.text: Actually accepting plaster at last for break

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: in fact = actually

indicators.note: at the last means at the very end, so only the final letter is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of plaster

explanation.surface: Someone really did take a plaster cast after a broken bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like a fracture to go with the plaster, but it is the verb: to break a rule.
explanation.definitionFit: To infract a law or agreement is to violate or breach it, a formal verb for breaking rules.

clue.text: Gypsy chosen to take part in film

indicators.note: taking part means being only a portion, so the letters are a part spanning other words

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A traveller selected to act in a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across the gap between the end of the first word and the start of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Psycho is Alfred Hitchcock's 1960 thriller, one of the most famous horror movies ever made.

clue.text: Teacher — homosexual, say

indicators.note: say means speak the words out, so we want what they sound like

parts.note: pupils address a male teacher as sir
gay = homosexual

explanation.surface: Describing a schoolmaster as gay.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken together, the schoolroom form of address and the word for homosexual give the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Sergei, as in Rachmaninov, is a common Russian first name, so a possible compatriot.

clue.text: Like a romantic dinner-dance till shattered

indicators.note: a shattered thing is broken into pieces that can be put back in any order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A romantic evening of dining and dancing that goes on until everyone is exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen ties 'dinner' to 'dance', but the definition ends at 'dinner' and 'dance' starts the material to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Romantic meals are stereotypically eaten by soft flame light from tapers on the table.

clue.text: Love writing, but missing a new opportunity

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: something missing has been left out, so letters are dropped

parts.note: penning = writing
N is the abbreviation for new; 'a' means just one of them

explanation.surface: Someone loves to write but lets a fresh chance pass.
explanation.walkthrough: Writing has two Ns; only one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An opening is a chance or vacancy, as in a job opening, so it is an everyday synonym.

clue.text: In villa, minder murdered

indicators.note: a murdered thing is violently destroyed, leaving the letters to be rebuilt in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bodyguard killed inside a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no definition; all thirteen letters of the first three words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble's one historic figure: the Bolshevik revolutionary who founded the Soviet state in 1917.

clue.text: Shakespeare's work initially making a comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the letters go back the way they came

parts.note: the initials of As You Like It, a Shakespeare comedy

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare play beginning to return to fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The work is not in the clue: you must think of a play whose title's first letters, run backwards, make a name. As You Like It fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Ilya, as in Repin the painter, is a Russian first name, so a possible compatriot.

clue.text: Athlete collapsed on narrow strip

parts.note: fell = collapsed, fell down
a runner is a long narrow rug or table cloth

explanation.surface: A sportsman who fell over on a narrow track.
explanation.walkthrough: A fell is a hill or moor in northern England, which is where fell running is done.
explanation.definitionFit: A fell runner is a sportsperson who races over hills and open upland country.

clue.text: County boundary area

parts.note: the river Tamar forms most of the border between Devon and Cornwall
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.walkthrough: The Tamar is a river in south-west England dividing the counties of Devon and Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Tamara is a Russian woman's first name, so a possible compatriot of Lenin.

clue.text: Cloth with pattern astrologer first worked out in secret

indicators.note: first means placed at the front, so this piece leads the other

parts.note: John Dee was Elizabeth I's astrologer and magician
plaid is tartan cloth, woven in a checked pattern

explanation.surface: A patterned fabric that a stargazer devised secretly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked out' suggests anagram, but it belongs to the definition with 'in secret'.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep-laid scheme is one carefully and covertly planned, like a plot hatched well in advance.

clue.text: A fight, not vicious — that's sweet

parts.note: taken as written
to spar is to box or fight
tame = gentle, not savage

explanation.surface: A gentle scrap, which is rather charming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an exclamation of approval, but it is the thing that sweetens.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspartame is an artificial sweetening agent used in diet drinks in place of sugar.

clue.text: It brings relief at one's rear, say, turning over (I mean it!)

parts.note: anal relates to the backside

indicators.note: to turn something over is to flip it, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: eg, for example, is what say means here
sic, Latin 'thus', marks a word as meant exactly as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark about relief arriving at the back end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is a common crossword stand-in for 'for example', EG. Sic is printed in brackets after a quoted word to show it was deliberate.
explanation.definitionFit: An analgesic is a painkiller, a drug that eases pain such as aspirin.

clue.text: Amputee's situation?

parts.note: surface reading: the circumstances of someone who has lost a limb
setter's reading: zero limbs below the hip, written with the letter for nought

explanation.walkthrough: Someone missing a limb might have no leg; write nought as the letter O and you have the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Oleg is a common Russian man's first name, so a possible compatriot of Lenin.

clue.text: As owned by tiny delivery company?

parts.words: As owned by tiny delivery company?
parts.note: surface reading: the possessions of a very small courier firm

parts.words: As owned by tiny delivery company?
parts.note: setter's reading: a fleet of one vehicle, with the roman numeral for one in front of the vehicle

explanation.surface: Wondering what a very small courier business possesses.
explanation.walkthrough: The roman numeral for one is I, so the firm's whole fleet is one van.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Ivan, as in the Terrible, is the classic Russian man's first name.

clue.text: Eavesdroppers with silent transport, we hear, heading off

indicators.note: a heading is the top or front, and off means removed, so the first letter goes
what we hear is what is spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: bicycles are noiseless transport; without their first letter they are said like the answer

explanation.surface: Snoopers who travel by quiet vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eavesdroppers' means snoopers, but read literally it is things that drop from the eaves. Bicycles lose the B, and what remains is pronounced the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Icicles hang from the edges of a roof and fall from the eaves, so they literally drop off them.

clue.text: Remarkably great pics that show extent of the damage

definitions.text: that show extent of the damage
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the things that show it

indicators.note: remarkably suggests something unusual or extraordinary, so the letters are put in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Striking photographs of a disaster scene revealing how bad the destruction was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The damage' is slang for what something costs, as in 'what's the damage?', not physical harm.
explanation.definitionFit: Labels on goods state their cost, and 'the damage' is an informal word for a bill.

clue.text: Autocratic state unknown to interfere with eccentric order

indicators.note: to interfere is to get in the way, so one piece pushes into the middle of another

parts.note: a card is an eccentric or amusing person
algebra uses x, y and z for unknowns
the OM is the Order of Merit

explanation.surface: A dictatorship meddling with a strange new arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric order' looks like an anagram, but each word gives its own piece. The Order of Merit is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Czardom is the realm or rule of a czar, the absolute monarch of Russia, so it describes an absolute regime.

clue.text: Pope's blood in short supply and in pale shade

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the word loses its final letter
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: grey is a pale, dull colour
gore is spilt blood, here missing its last letter

explanation.surface: An anaemic pontiff, low on blood and looking pale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope's' reads as possessive but is 'Pope is', the definition followed by a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sixteen popes took the name Gregory, among them Gregory the Great and Gregory XIII of the calendar.

clue.text: In Scotland, own up pinching gear

indicators.note: to pinch is to grip tightly, so one piece holds another inside it
in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, running backwards

parts.note: ain is the Scots word for own
kit = equipment, gear

explanation.surface: A Scot confesses to stealing equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Own up' looks like confessing, but 'up' is the reversal signal for the Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Nikita, as in Khrushchev, is a Russian man's first name, so a possible compatriot.

clue.text: Run indoors to grab good sort of seat

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: grabbing means seizing hold, so one piece is clutched inside another

parts.note: inside = indoors
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Dashing inside to claim a decent chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good sort of seat' tempts as the definition, but 'good' is the piece taken inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringside seat is in the front row beside a boxing ring or circus ring, giving a close view.

clue.text: A word that links religious education with me, subjectively

parts.note: and is the commonest joining word
RE is the school subject Religious Education
me used as the subject of a sentence becomes I

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson connecting religious study with the speaker's own view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subjectively' seems to mean from a personal viewpoint, but it is grammatical: me in the subject case.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Andrei, as in Tarkovsky, is a Russian man's first name, so a possible compatriot.

clue.text: Stop: one son's missing, I believe

definitions.note: what a believer would say; the answer is the noun for such a person

indicators.note: missing means absent, so letters are taken out

parts.note: desist = stop
S is the abbreviation for son; one of the two in the word is removed

explanation.surface: A parent halting proceedings because one boy has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb to remove from has two Ss; only one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A deist believes in a creator God but not revelation, so 'I believe' is the deist's creed.

clue.text: Pupils I gave dinner to around one in secret

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a class is a group of pupils
taken as written
to feed someone is to give them a meal
I is the roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A teacher secretly treating students to a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In secret' looks like part of the story, but 'in' is a link and 'secret' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Classified documents are officially restricted, kept confidential for reasons of national security.

clue.text: Tax collectors once full of energy

indicators.note: a thing full of something holds it inside

parts.note: IR is the Inland Revenue, the former British tax authority
go = energy, vigour

explanation.surface: Past taxmen who were brimming with vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue merged into HMRC in 2005, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Igor, as in Stravinsky, is a Russian man's first name, so a possible compatriot.

clue.text: Spies infiltrating very Liberal party

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to slip inside an organisation, so one piece enters another

parts.note: so = very
L is the abbreviation for Liberal
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: Secret agents worming into a thoroughly Liberal political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal party' reads as a political party, but 'party' alone is the definition, a gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A social is an informal gathering or get-together, held by a club or group for fun.

clue.text: Forbidding alcohol around US university

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a dry state or event bans alcohol
MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: An American campus that bans drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: MIT, in Massachusetts, is the usual crossword US university.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this undefined: Dmitry, as in Mendeleev, is a Russian man's first name, so a possible compatriot.
